title: Planning and zoning restrictions (ACT)
summary: The ACT's planning system, under the Planning Act 2023 (ACT), decides what may be built where: zoning limits the number and type of homes and the sites open to shops and other businesses, and development approvals add time and cost.

instruments.title: Planning Act 2023 (ACT)
instruments.provisions: planning schemes, zoning and development approval

direction_rationale: Restrictive zoning holds the supply of housing below demand, so prices sit well above the cost of building; the Productivity Commission estimates housing regulation costs about 1% of GDP a year, with zoning the largest part. Zoning and approvals also limit where new businesses can open; the Harper Review said planning rules should not restrict competition unless the benefits outweigh the costs.

assessment.summary: Zoning and planning approvals limit how many homes can be built and where businesses can open. They push house prices far above the cost of building, add delays and paperwork, and can shelter existing businesses from new rivals. The Productivity Commission puts the cost of housing regulation at about 1% of GDP a year, mostly from zoning.

marks.reason: Zoning keeps house prices well above the cost of supply: a large distortion in the largest asset market.
Zoning and approvals limit the sites open to new businesses; the Harper Review found planning rules can favour incumbents.
Development approvals add paperwork, holding costs and delay to building homes and business premises.

assessment.confidence_note: No city estimate of the zoning premium was found for this jurisdiction; the marks rest on the Productivity Commission's national estimate and the common design of planning systems.
